VOICEOVER:

Leaders of top AI companies say the artificial-intelligence industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up.

Without such a slowdown, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI could be capable within six to 12 months of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet.

Amodei also offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, one part of which he said Anthropic is undertaking by itself already.

Some big names in the AI industry offered quick support, including OpenAI's Sam Altman, who said the company would delay its planned IPO beyond 2026.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, meanwhile, said on X that “Dario is right.”

Amodei's comments follow a high-profile resignation earlier in the week by Jacob Coxon, who said that both Anthropic and OpenAI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Amodei said he still believes in the tremendous benefits that AI could create, such as cures for major diseases.

But he said he has grown more worried over the last few months about AI’s growing ability to improve itself and build the next generation of AI.
STORYLINE:
Leaders of top AI companies say the artificial-intelligence industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up.

Without such a slowdown, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI could be capable within six to 12 months of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet.



SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, meanwhile, said on X that “Dario is right.”

recentItems.title: Swedish voters go to polls to choose a new parliament as hard right bids for role in government
recentItems.description:
(13 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTIONS SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Nacka, Stockholm County, Sweden -  13 September 2026
1. Various of voters in polling station
2. Pan of voter going to voting booth
3. Voters in voting booth
4. Pan of ballot papers
5. SOUNDBITE (English) Anna Envall, voter:
"I hope there is going to be change here in Sweden, I would like climate to be a bigger topic and immigration."
6. Various of voters registering and election workers casting their ballots
7. SOUNDBITE (English) Claes Lithagen, voter:
"The most important thing is unemployment rate in Sweden which is very high, I think it is around third or fourth highest in Europe, so that's one very important thing to solve in some way."
8. Various of voters going to voting booth
9. . Various of voters registering and election workers casting their ballots
STORYLINE:
Voters in Sweden headed to the polls on Sunday for an election that will determine whether a conservative leader remains in charge and a hard-right party wins ministerial jobs for the first time, or whether the centre-left returns to power.

Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson is seeking a second four-year term at the helm of the European Union (EU) nation that is also NATO’s newest member. 

Meanwhile, his predecessor hopes to win the job back.

Experts say the campaign has been fragmented and incoherent, with policy questions such as how healthcare should be organized drowned out by questions about which parties will be able to put together a government.

Kristersson has led Sweden since 2022 with a three-party centre-right coalition. 

It relies on outside support from the Sweden Democrats, an anti-immigration party that has far-right roots but has moved toward the political mainstream, for a parliamentary majority. 

If the right is reelected, it can expect Cabinet posts this time.

He’s up against Magdalena Andersson of the centre-left Social Democrats, a party that more often than not has led Swedish governments since World War II. 

Andersson served as prime minister from 2021 until she lost power at the last election.

There are two major political blocs: one with four parties on the right and another with four parties on the left. 

So the big question is less about which party wins and more about which side can form a majority. 

Individual parties need a minimum of 4% of the vote to win parliamentary seats.

More than 8 million people in the nation of about 10.6 million are eligible to vote in the election for the 349-seat parliament, the Riksdag, which will elect the next prime minister. 

The Swedish Election Authority says the first preliminary results will be available around 9 p.m. (1900 GMT).

recentItems.title: Brazil experiences a cultural surge as celebrities and tourists embrace its vibrant culture
recentItems.description:
(13 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Rio de Janeiro, Brazil - 2 September 2026
1. Various of foreign tourists wearing Brazil’s national soccer jersey posing for photos at viewpoint in Rocinha favela
2. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) Eduardo Maristany, 30, Spanish tourist: 
“We saw all these videos on social media about the favelas, the beaches, the atmosphere, the parties, the women, a little of everything.”
3. Vitor Oliveira, tourist guide in Rocinha, talking to group of tourists
4. SOUNDBITE (Portuguese) Vitor Oliveira, tour guide: 
“I think social media is the main way to get information out to the world quickly and widely. Without it, I think only the local residents would be here, this huge number of tourists wouldn’t be here.”
5. Various of tourists wearing Brazil's jersey walking through favela
6. Tourists watching performance
7. Italian tourist Edda Di Dato dancing with locals
8. SOUNDBITE (Italian) Edda Di Dato, 26, Italian tourist: 
“I really like the scenery, the way they (Brazilians) live, and their laid-back lifestyle. I like how they are, they're very friendly, and they make me feel at ease.”
9. Various of bars aimed at tourists in Rocinha
10. Various of spot popular on social media where tourists get drone video of them with view
11. Tilt up of Rocinha favela 
STORYLINE:
Brazil is having a moment. Celebrities and record numbers of tourists donning green, yellow and blue are flooding into the country. 

Brazilian culture - from its Oscar nominated films to funk music - is taking the world by storm. 

Global fashion brands and influencers are leaning into the hype.

For decades, Brazilians have lamented that the country and its cultural makeup and output have long gone under-appreciated in what has become known as the “mongrel complex.”

But as attention from abroad pours in and consolidates itself in 2026, some say a shift may be underway with the rise of “caramelo pride” — a ubiquitous celebration by Brazilians of caramel-colored street mutts that have come to represent the country.

Brazil has captured the world’s attention and admiration before, and Brazilians cyclically observe that “Brasil está na moda,” or Brazil is in fashion.

Many trace the current popularity of the phase to 2023, when Brazilcore - a fashion trend featuring the colors of the Brazilian flag and inspired by Brazilian culture - gained widespread global traction. 

Celebrities including Emily Ratajkowski, Hailey Bieber, Tina Kunakey, Sabrina Carpenter, Alex Consani and Addison Rae have all participated in the trend. 

Recently, the popularity of Brazilcore has morphed into a massive, multi-faceted global phenomenon that celebrates “brasilidade,” or Brazilianness, moving beyond fashion to include music, dance, cinema and sport.

Brazilcore can be spotted on high streets around the world and takes the forms of bikinis, micro-shorts, crochet pieces, soccer shirts and accessories.

Brands including fast fashion giants, such as Zara and H&M, have put out green and yellow tops emblazoned with Rio de Janeiro, while Chanel, Jil Sander and Schiaparelli have all made references to Brazil’s national colors. 

The hype around Brazil has also translated into record numbers of tourists visiting the country.

More than 9 million tourists came to Brazil last year, a 37% increase compared to 2024. 

Jokes on the internet abound about the CPF - an individual’s fiscal identity in Brazil - being the new sought-after green card.


These videos have gone viral in recent months.



It’s not just tourists who are engaging with Brazil.

recentItems.title: Israeli airstrike hits car in Gaza City killing 2 people, al-Shifa hospital says
recentItems.description:
(13 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

++VIDEO CONTAINS FOOTAGE OF BLOOD++

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Gaza City, Gaza Strip - 13 September 2026
1. Children gathering near car destroyed by Israeli airstrike 
2. Various of smoke billowing from destroyed car, blood on the ground  ++ CONTAINS FOOTAGE OF BLOOD++
3. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Ahmad Shreim, resident of Gaza City:
"I was at home when I heard the sound of the strike. I ran to the scene and found two mangled bodies—severed remains; there was nothing left from the chest up—no heads. Nowhere was it safe. I ran out to check on my daughter, fearing for her safety, as she was at kindergarten. There is no safe place in Gaza; there is nothing. Our life is full of fear."
4. Various of smoke rising from destroyed car
5. Various of wrapped bodies of people killed 
STORYLINE:
An Israeli strike on Sunday hit a car in Gaza City, killing two people, according to Shifa Hospital, which received the bodies.

Ahmad Shreim, who was on his way to pick up his daughter from school, said he arrived at the scene and saw only body parts.

“They had no heads,” he said, adding that he felt “nowhere is safe” in Gaza. 

“Our life is full of fear.”

The Israeli military said it was aware of the strike and that it targeted two Hamas members.

Sunday’s casualties were the latest among Palestinians in Gaza since an October fragile ceasefire deal attempted to halt a more than two-year war between Israel and Hamas.

While the heaviest fighting has subsided since a ceasefire took hold in October, Israeli forces have carried out repeated airstrikes, killing 1,369 Palestinians, according to health officials in Gaza.

AP Production by: Wafaa Shurafa

(13 Sep 2026) 
IRAQ SHOPPING FESTIVAL

SOURCE: ASSOCIATED PRESS

RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Baghdad, Iraq  - 7 September 2026
1. Various of women checking displayed items
2. People visiting the shopping festival 
3. Various of people looking at accessories 
4. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Hazim Hashim, visitor from Baghdad:
“It is a nice initiative; to get to know to other cultures and to check out into many things. Not everyone goes to Shorija (main market in Baghdad) or other main shopping places like that. But, here you can find everything, you can find clothes, honey and many other things.”

5. Various of handmade baskets at the Iranian section 
7. Various of women looking at cooking pans 
8. Various of spices displayed at Yemen’s section
9. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Abdulrahman al-Hashidi, representative of Yemeni spices company:
“Well, the festival is amazing, and the costumers’ turnout is big. The purchasing power is very strong as well. I mean I would consider it being one of the best exhibitions compared to Gulf countries.”

10. Various of people looking at displayed handicrafts, 
11. Man playing a traditional drum
11. Syrian Aleppo soap section 
12. Various of Kuwaiti and Emirati perfume sections 
13. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Ali Muhanad, representative of Emirati perfume company:
“We came and participated in Baghdad expo because the turnout is very nice. People’s turnout at the expo is big, and they have been lovely. Regarding the festival, the shopping is going well, and the turnout is good at the same time, and the costumer won't face any difficulties here.”

14. Various of people passing by toys section 
15. Top shot of people inside the shopping festival 
16. Wide of visitors at festival’s entry gate
STORYLINE:
From Yemeni spices to Emiratis perfumes, a festival brought the entire Middle East to Baghdad.

The shopping festival in the Iraqi capital bustled with visitors eager to shop a variety of international and local offerings. 

People wandered different sections, looking at handmade items such as embroidered tablecloths and woven baskets, while others shopped for drums and lively decorations. 

Some sampled a variety of spices and sweets, and tried out famous olive oil soup from Aleppo, Syria. 

Abdulrahman al-Hashidi, a representative of Yemeni spices company, said the turnout to his section has been high, with many wanting to grab some authentic spices from his country.

Customers said they enjoyed exploring many cultures in one space. 

"Here you can find everything,” said Hazim Hashim, a visitor from Baghdad.

The festival, which is held at the Baghdad International Fair ground, ends on 13 September.

AP video by Ali Jabar

recentItems.title: Rescuers pull more bodies from burned Philippine ferry as death toll rises
recentItems.description:
(13 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Coron, Palawan province , Philippines -  13 September 2026
1. Various of grounded burnt ferry MV June Aster near an island in Palawan 
2. Burnt ferry pan right to Philippine Coast Guard vessel approaching beside another ship 
3. Wide of Coast Guard ship 
4. Body bags containing some of the retrieved remains of ferry fire 
5.  Various of body bags 
6. Philippine Coast Guard helicopter taking off 
7. Wide of helicopter taking off 
8. Various of Coast Guard boat 
9. Wide of Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab beside tv screen showing the data of the ferry fire 
10. SOUNDBITE (English) Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson:
 “The total number of survivors 43, we put here the not on board because they are not included the ticket manifest just to be… we have the full accounting of the number. So not on board is the two and then missing is 13, the fatality is 76.” 
11. Shipping line representative (left) with Coast Guard officials  
12. SOUNDBITE (English) Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson:
“The additional 41 cadavers that were retrieved yesterday will be transferred to BPR Cape Engaño and to be transported to port of Borac today.”
13. Various of bodybags being unloaded from Coast Guard ship 
14. Medical workers carrying body bags of ferry fire victims on stretcher 
15. Wide of medical workers carrying stretchers 
16. Medical workers arranging bodybags beside tent for forensic processing     
STORYLINE:
Rescuers retrieved more remains from a passenger ferry in the Philippines that was gutted by fire, bringing the death toll on Saturday to 76 with 13 missing.

Forty-three people survived the fire on Wednesday night among the 132 on board.

The ferry sailed from the capital, Manila, and was some 39 kilometers (24 miles) from its destination in Coron, in southwestern Palawan province, when the fire erupted.

The cause has not been determined but the coast guard spokesperson quoted a survivor as saying it may have started from the cargo hold. The survivor recounted hearing a blast, with smoke and fire quickly spreading, fanned by the winds, officials said.

Tents were put up in the Port of Borac in Coron, where body bags were brought down from a ship that transported them from the ferry.

Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, the coast guard spokesperson, said authorities were looking for the ship's captain, who reportedly survived but is not listed among the survivors.

The multi-agency maritime safety and criminal investigations will look into all angles, and the possible liability of the captain and crew, she added.

Cayabyab said survivors recounted the fire spread quickly, with no time to get life jackets. 

A tarpaulin that shielded the open areas of the ship from the rain “may be a possible contributing factor but we can’t determine now if they were trapped inside,” she added.

Investigators will also check if fire emergency procedures were followed, including if the captain sounded an alarm or gave a warning and instructions, and if the crew assisted the passengers.

Ferries are frequently used for transport in the Philippine archipelago. 

Sea accidents are not uncommon due to storms, badly maintained vessels, overcrowding and spotty enforcement of safety regulations, especially in remote provinces.

In 1987, the ferry Dona Paz sank after colliding with a fuel tanker in the central Philippines, killing more than 4,300 people in the world’s deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.

2. Various of Andersson registering and election workers casting her ballot
3. SOUNDBITE (English) Magdalena Andersson, leader of Social Democrats:
"It's up to the Swedish people now and we will have the election result tonight. But of course, this is very important election for Sweden, if we for the first time should have a right-wing extremist party founded by Neo-Nazis in our government or if the government should be led by me."
4. Various of voters in voting booth

STORYLINE:
Voters in Sweden are going to the polls on Sunday for an election that will determine whether a conservative leader remains in charge and a hard-right party wins ministerial jobs for the first time, or whether the center-left returns to power.

Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson is seeking a second four-year term at the helm of the European Union nation that is also NATO’s newest member. Meanwhile, his predecessor hopes to win the job back. 

Experts say the campaign has been fragmented and incoherent, with policy questions such as how healthcare should be organized drowned out by the question of which parties will be able to put together a government.

“Crime has come down, inflation has come down. So these topics are not really what people discuss,” said Zeth Isaksson, a sociologist in electoral behavior at Stockholm University and a political scientist at the European University Institute in Florence, Italy. “People discuss who is going to be in government, and that’s what the election is about.” 

Kristersson has led Sweden since 2022 with a three-party center-right coalition. It relies on outside support from the Sweden Democrats, an anti-immigration party that has far-right roots but has moved toward the political mainstream, for a parliamentary majority. If the right is reelected, it can expect Cabinet posts this time.

He’s up against Magdalena Andersson of the center-left Social Democrats, a party that more often than not has led Swedish governments since World War II. Andersson served as prime minister from 2021 until she lost power at the last election.

There are two major political blocs: one with four parties on the right and another with four parties on the left. So the big question is not so much which party wins as which side can put together a majority. Individual parties need a minimum 4% of the vote to win parliamentary seats.

The Sweden Democrats, who in 2022 took 20.5% of the vote to become the biggest party on the right, can expect Cabinet seats if power doesn’t change hands. 

Kristersson announced in April that his conservative Moderates would allow them into government if the right has a majority — though he would remain prime minister even if the Sweden Democrats are the stronger party.

The Sweden Democrats were founded in the 1980s by people who had been active in right-wing extremist groups, including neo-Nazis. They toned down their rhetoric and expelled openly racist members under Jimmie Åkesson, who has led them since 2005 and overseen their growth from what was once a marginal party. 

The Sweden Democrats' role is in focus against a background of gains for the populist right in Europe, including the first-place finish by the far-right Alternative for Germany party in a regional election there Sept. 6.
